theory.intro: When both sides vary, an absolute value inequality cannot be split by a single rule. Sketch $y = |f(x)|$ and $y = g(x)$ and read where one lies above the other, or split into cases where an expression inside the bars is $0$.
facts: When both sides are absolute values, $|f(x)| \le |g(x)|$ means $[f(x)]^2 \le [g(x)]^2$, so $[f(x) - g(x)][f(x) + g(x)] \le 0$.
Do not square $|f(x)| < g(x)$ unless $g(x) > 0$, because squaring adds false solutions where $g(x)$ is negative.
**Case analysis** splits at $f(x) = 0$: use $|f(x)| = f(x)$ where $f(x) \ge 0$, and $|f(x)| = -f(x)$ where $f(x) < 0$.
A solution found in one case must be intersected with that case's own condition on $x$.
Graphically, solve $f(x) = g(x)$ and $-f(x) = g(x)$ for the intersections, then read off where $|f(x)|$ is above or below $g(x)$.
Since $|x - a| > 0$ for all $x \neq a$, multiplying by $|x - a|$ never reverses the inequality.
steps: Choose an appropriate method: squaring both sides (if both sides are absolute values), case analysis, or graphical sketching.
For case analysis, split the domain at the critical values where expressions inside absolute value bars equal $0$.
Solve the resulting algebraic inequality in each case.
Intersect each case solution with its defining domain condition.
Take the union of the valid solutions from all cases to form the complete solution set.

foundation.solution_text:
For $x \ge 3$:
$x - 3 < x + 5 \implies -3 < 5$, true for all $x \ge 3$.
For $x < 3$:
$-(x - 3) < x + 5$
$-x + 3 < x + 5$
$-2x < 2 \implies x > -1$
Interval: $-1 < x < 3$.
Combining both cases:
$x > -1$

For $x \ge \dfrac{5}{2}$:
$2x - 5 > x \implies x > 5$
For $x < \dfrac{5}{2}$:
$-(2x - 5) > x$
$-2x + 5 > x$
$-3x > -5 \implies x < \dfrac{5}{3}$
Combining cases:
$x < \dfrac{5}{3}$ or $x > 5$

For $x \ge -\dfrac{2}{3}$:
$3x + 2 \le 2x + 5 \implies x \le 3$
Interval: $-\dfrac{2}{3} \le x \le 3$.
For $x < -\dfrac{2}{3}$:
$-(3x + 2) \le 2x + 5$
$-3x - 2 \le 2x + 5$
$-5x \le 7 \implies x \ge -\dfrac{7}{5}$
Interval: $-\dfrac{7}{5} \le x < -\dfrac{2}{3}$.
Combining cases:
$-\dfrac{7}{5} \le x \le 3$

development.solution_text:
Square both sides:
$(2x + 1)^2 \le (x - 5)^2$
$4x^2 + 4x + 1 \le x^2 - 10x + 25$
$3x^2 + 14x - 24 \le 0$
$(3x - 4)(x + 6) \le 0$
Critical values: $x = -6, \dfrac{4}{3}$.
$-6 \le x \le \dfrac{4}{3}$

For $x \ge \dfrac{3}{4}$:
$4x - 3 > 2x + 3 \implies 2x > 6 \implies x > 3$
For $x < \dfrac{3}{4}$:
$-(4x - 3) > 2x + 3$
$-4x + 3 > 2x + 3$
$-6x > 0 \implies x < 0$
Combining cases:
$x < 0$ or $x > 3$

$-4 < x^2 - 5 < 4$
$1 < x^2 < 9$
Taking square roots:
$-3 < x < -1$ or $1 < x < 3$

Restriction: $x \neq 2$.
Since $|x - 2| > 0$, multiply by $3|x - 2|$:
$x|x - 2| \ge 3$
For $x > 2$:
$x(x - 2) \ge 3 \implies x^2 - 2x - 3 \ge 0 \implies (x - 3)(x + 1) \ge 0$
Since $x > 2$, this gives $x \ge 3$.
For $x < 2$:
$-x(x - 2) \ge 3 \implies -x^2 + 2x \ge 3 \implies x^2 - 2x + 3 \le 0$
Discriminant $\Delta = 4 - 12 = -8 < 0$, no real solution.
$x \ge 3$

Since LHS $\ge 0$, $3x > 0 \implies x > 0$.
For $x > 0$, $x + \dfrac{1}{x} > 0$, so $\left|x + \dfrac{1}{x}\right| = x + \dfrac{1}{x}$.
$x + \dfrac{1}{x} < 3x$
$\dfrac{1}{x} < 2x$
Multiply by $x > 0$:
$1 < 2x^2$
$x^2 > \dfrac{1}{2}$
Since $x > 0$:
$x > \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

mastery.solution_text:
Restriction: $x \neq 4$.
Multiply by $|x - 4| > 0$:
$(5 - x)|x - 4| > 1$
For $x > 4$:
$(5 - x)(x - 4) > 1 \implies -x^2 + 9x - 20 > 1 \implies x^2 - 9x + 21 < 0$
Discriminant $\Delta = 81 - 84 = -3 < 0$, no real solution.
For $x < 4$:
$-(5 - x)(x - 4) > 1 \implies (x - 5)(x - 4) > 1 \implies x^2 - 9x + 20 > 1 \implies x^2 - 9x + 19 > 0$
Roots: $x = \dfrac{9 \pm \sqrt{5}}{2}$.
Intersecting $x < \dfrac{9 - \sqrt{5}}{2}$ or $x > \dfrac{9 + \sqrt{5}}{2}$ with $x < 4$:
$x < \dfrac{9 - \sqrt{5}}{2}$

Since $|x^2 - 3x| \ge 0$, we require $2x > 0 \implies x > 0$.
Split into double inequality:
$-2x < x^2 - 3x < 2x$
Left inequality:
$x^2 - 3x > -2x \implies x^2 - x > 0 \implies x(x - 1) > 0$
Since $x > 0$, this requires $x > 1$.
Right inequality:
$x^2 - 3x < 2x \implies x^2 - 5x < 0 \implies x(x - 5) < 0$
This gives $0 < x < 5$.
Intersecting $x > 1$ and $0 < x < 5$:
$1 < x < 5$
